import Mathlib
/-! QED-M075: Break the 5/8 barrier for primes with triply well-factorable weights
Primes are equidistributed in residue classes on average over moduli q up to x^{5/8-ε} when the
average is weighted by triply well-factorable weights (Pascadi 2025). The problem is to push the
exponent beyond 5/8.
Informal statement: Say (λ_q)_{q ≤ Q} is triply well-factorable of level Q if for all Q₁Q₂Q₃ = Q
there are 1-bounded α, β, γ supported on q_i ≤ Q_i with λ = α * β * γ (Dirichlet convolution).
Let θ* be the sup of θ such that for all ε, A > 0, fixed a ≠ 0, and every such λ of level
Q = x^{θ-ε}: ∑_{q ≤ Q, (q,a)=1} λ_q (π(x;q,a) − π(x)/φ(q)) ≪_{ε,A,a} x (log x)^{-A}.
Known θ* ≥ 5/8 (Pascadi). Prove θ* > 5/8.
Formalization notes: Weights are complex. "Triply well-factorable of level Q" requires, for every
real Q₁, Q₂, Q₃ ≥ 1 with Q₁Q₂Q₃ = Q, sequences α, β, γ with |·| ≤ 1 supported on [1, Q_i] whose
triple Dirichlet convolution is λ (so λ is automatically supported on [1, Q]). π(x;q,a) counts primes
p ≤ x with p ≡ a (mod q); π(x) counts primes p ≤ x; φ = Nat.totient. The implied constant C and the
threshold x₀ may depend on θ, ε, A, a but must be uniform in λ. Since the property for θ implies it
for every smaller θ (absorb θ − θ' into ε), "θ* > 5/8" is equivalent to the existence of some
θ > 5/8 with the property, which is what `Claim` says. Proving `Claim` breaks the 5/8 barrier;
proving `¬ Claim` would show that 5/8 is the true limit for this class of weights (a barrier
theorem). Known: the property holds for θ = 5/8 (Pascadi, arXiv:2505.00653, Thm 1.3).
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM075

/-- `α` is 1-bounded and supported on integers in `[1, Q]`. -/
def BoundedSupported (Q : ℝ) (α : ℕ → ℂ) : Prop :=
  (∀ n : ℕ, ‖α n‖ ≤ 1) ∧ (∀ n : ℕ, α n ≠ 0 → 1 ≤ n ∧ (n : ℝ) ≤ Q)

/-- Triple Dirichlet convolution `(α * β * γ)(q) = ∑_{abc = q} α(a) β(b) γ(c)`. -/
noncomputable def conv3 (α β γ : ℕ → ℂ) (q : ℕ) : ℂ :=
  ∑ a ∈ q.divisors, ∑ b ∈ (q / a).divisors, α a * β b * γ (q / a / b)

/-- Triply well-factorable weights of level `Q`. -/
def TriplyWellFactorable (Q : ℝ) (w : ℕ → ℂ) : Prop :=
  ∀ Q₁ Q₂ Q₃ : ℝ, 1 ≤ Q₁ → 1 ≤ Q₂ → 1 ≤ Q₃ → Q₁ * Q₂ * Q₃ = Q →
    ∃ α β γ : ℕ → ℂ, BoundedSupported Q₁ α ∧ BoundedSupported Q₂ β ∧ BoundedSupported Q₃ γ ∧
      ∀ q : ℕ, w q = conv3 α β γ q

open Classical in
/-- `π(x)`: number of primes `p ≤ x`. -/
noncomputable def primeCount (x : ℝ) : ℕ :=
  ((Finset.range (⌊x⌋₊ + 1)).filter (fun p => Nat.Prime p)).card

open Classical in
/-- `π(x; q, a)`: number of primes `p ≤ x` with `p ≡ a (mod q)`. -/
noncomputable def primeCountAP (x : ℝ) (q : ℕ) (a : ℤ) : ℕ :=
  ((Finset.range (⌊x⌋₊ + 1)).filter
    (fun p => Nat.Prime p ∧ (p : ℤ) % (q : ℤ) = a % (q : ℤ))).card

/-- `π(x;q,a) − π(x)/φ(q)`. -/
noncomputable def discrepancy (x : ℝ) (q : ℕ) (a : ℤ) : ℝ :=
  (primeCountAP x q a : ℝ) - (primeCount x : ℝ) / (Nat.totient q : ℝ)

open Classical in
/-- The weighted sum `∑_{q ≤ Q, (q,a)=1} w_q (π(x;q,a) − π(x)/φ(q))`. -/
noncomputable def weightedSum (x Q : ℝ) (a : ℤ) (w : ℕ → ℂ) : ℂ :=
  ∑ q ∈ ((Finset.Icc 1 ⌊Q⌋₊ : Finset ℕ).filter (fun q : ℕ => Int.gcd (q : ℤ) a = 1)),
    w q * ((discrepancy x q a : ℝ) : ℂ)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ θ : ℝ, 5 / 8 < θ ∧
    ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∀ A : ℝ, 0 < A → ∀ a : ℤ, a ≠ 0 →
      ∃ C x₀ : ℝ, ∀ x : ℝ, x₀ ≤ x → ∀ w : ℕ → ℂ,
        TriplyWellFactorable (x ^ (θ - ε)) w →
          ‖weightedSum x (x ^ (θ - ε)) a w‖ ≤ C * x * (Real.log x) ^ (-A)

end OpenProblems.QEDM075
prov_reason: Passing the 5/8 exponent for triply well-factorable weights is the explicit frontier identified by Pascadi (who calls 5/8 the apparent limit of current technology), following Lichtman's work; QED only packages it.

title: Close the gap in the density of integers that are sums of two rational cubes
credit: Alpöge, Bhargava, Shnidman, Integers expressible as the sum of two rational cubes, arXiv:2210.10730 (2022); Koymans-Smith arXiv:2606.06024 (2026) for the complement side.

plain: BSD plus the minimalist rank heuristic predict that exactly half of all integers are sums of two rational cubes. Proven: at least 2/21 are (Alpöge–Bhargava–Shnidman), and at least 31.95% are not (Koymans–Smith). Improve either bound.
math: Let $\mathcal S=\{n\in\mathbb Z: n=x^3+y^3,\ x,y\in\mathbb Q\}$ and $d_\pm$ the lower densities of $\mathcal S$ and of its complement (ordered by $|n|$). Known: $\underline d(\mathcal S)\ge 2/21$, $\underline d(\mathcal S^c)\ge 0.3195$. Conjecture: both densities equal $1/2$. Improve either constant.

BSD plus rank heuristics predict that half of all integers are sums of two rational cubes. Proven: at least 2/21 are (Alpöge-Bhargava-Shnidman) and at least 31.95% are not (Koymans-Smith). This file asks to improve the 2/21.
Informal statement: Let $\mathcal S=\{n\in\mathbb Z: n=x^3+y^3,\ x,y\in\mathbb Q\}$ and $d_\pm$ the lower densities of $\mathcal S$ and of its complement (ordered by $|n|$). Known: $\underline d(\mathcal S)\ge 2/21$, $\underline d(\mathcal S^c)\ge 0.3195$. Conjecture: both densities equal $1/2$. Improve either constant.

namespace OpenProblems.QEDM076

/-- `n` is a sum of two rational cubes. -/
def IsSumTwoRatCubes (n : ℕ) : Prop := ∃ x y : ℚ, (n : ℚ) = x ^ 3 + y ^ 3

/-- The number of `n ∈ [1, N]` that are sums of two rational cubes. -/
noncomputable def countS (N : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  Nat.card {n : ℕ // 1 ≤ n ∧ n ≤ N ∧ IsSumTwoRatCubes n}

def Claim : Prop :=

end OpenProblems.QEDM076
prov_reason: Improving the Alpöge-Bhargava-Shnidman proportions toward the conjectured 1/2 is the natural open problem stated in that line of work.

title: Improve H_1 <= 12 under EH alone
credit: D.H.J. Polymath 2014, arXiv:1407.4897; J. Maynard 2015, arXiv:1311.4600
plain: Assuming Elliott–Halberstam, Maynard's sieve gives infinitely many pairs of primes at distance at most 12. The generalized conjecture GEH gives 6. Lower 12 using EH alone.

/-! QED-M078: Improve H_1 ≤ 12 under EH alone
Assuming the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture, Maynard's sieve gives infinitely many pairs of primes at
distance at most 12 (GEH gives 6). Lower 12 using EH alone.
Informal statement: Let H₁ = liminf_n (p_{n+1} − p_n). Assuming EH (level θ = 1 − ε for every ε > 0,
for the von Mangoldt function only, not GEH), prove H₁ ≤ 10. (The alternative "prove that no
Selberg/Maynard-type sieve weight using EH alone can give H₁ < 12" concerns a class of methods and is
not formalized.)

max is encoded by quantifying over every choice function a(q) of residues coprime to q (equivalent).
H₁ ≤ 10 ⇔ infinitely many primes p with another prime in (p, p+10].

proving H₁ ≤ 10 also proves Claim). Proving `¬Claim` would require proving EH and H₁ > 10, i.e. is
not a realistic route. Caution for reviewers: if `EH` were mis-stated so as to be false, Claim would
be vacuous; the statement here is the standard one (θ < 1/2 is Bombieri–Vinogradov).
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM078

/-- ψ(x; q, a). -/
noncomputable def psiAP (x : ℝ) (q a : ℕ) : ℝ :=
  ∑ n ∈ (Finset.Icc 1 ⌊x⌋₊).filter (fun n => n % q = a % q), ArithmeticFunction.vonMangoldt n

/-- ψ(x). -/
noncomputable def psi (x : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∑ n ∈ Finset.Icc 1 ⌊x⌋₊, ArithmeticFunction.vonMangoldt n

/-- The Elliott–Halberstam conjecture. -/
def EH : Prop :=
  ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∀ A : ℝ, 0 < A → ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ x : ℝ, 2 ≤ x →
    ∀ a : ℕ → ℕ, (∀ q, Nat.Coprime (a q) q) →
      ∑ q ∈ Finset.Icc 1 ⌊x ^ (1 - ε)⌋₊,
          |psiAP x q (a q) - psi x / (Nat.totient q : ℝ)| ≤ C * x / Real.log x ^ A

def Claim : Prop :=
  EH → ∀ N : ℕ, ∃ p q : ℕ, N < p ∧ p.Prime ∧ q.Prime ∧ p < q ∧ q ≤ p + 10

end OpenProblems.QEDM078

title: Interval-sieve extremal bounds behind the Banks–Ford–Tao gap prediction
credit: Banks, Ford, Tao, Large prime gaps and probabilistic models, Invent. Math. 2023 (arXiv:1908.08613)

finite set of primes only finitely many Markov numbers are built from those primes alone.
Informal statement: Let 𝓜 = {m ≥ 1 : ∃ x, y ∈ ℤ_{>0}, x² + y² + m² = 3xym} and P(m) the largest

namespace OpenProblems.QEDM080

/-- `m` is a Markov number. -/
def IsMarkov (m : ℕ) : Prop :=

title: Lower the exponent 0.7785 for A4-quartic fields
credit: Bhargava, Shankar, Taniguchi, Thorne, Tsimerman, Zhao, 'Bounds on 2-torsion in class groups of number fields and integral points on elliptic curves', JAMS 2020 (arXiv:1701.02458, Thm 1.4); Loughran-Paterson arXiv:2510.05248

arXiv:2602.23619 (Alberts-Bucur, 2026 preprint): cited only for the status 'no 2026 improvement'.
plain: Malle predicts about X^{1/2} log X quartic fields with Galois group A4 and discriminant up to X. Loughran–Paterson (2025) proved the matching lower bound. The best upper bound is still about X^{0.7785}. Lower the exponent.

import Mathlib
/-! QED-M081: Lower the exponent 0.7785 for A4-quartic fields
Let N_{A4}(X) be the number of quartic number fields with Galois group A4 and |discriminant| ≤ X.
Malle predicts N_{A4}(X) ~ c X^{1/2} log X; Loughran-Paterson proved the matching lower bound.
The best upper bound is N_{A4}(X) ≪ X^{0.7784...+ε} (Bhargava-Shankar-Taniguchi-Thorne-Tsimerman-
Zhao). Lower this exponent.
Informal statement: Let N_{A4}(X) count quartic L/ℚ with Gal(L̃/ℚ) ≅ A4 and |Δ_L| ≤ X. Prove
N_{A4}(X) ≪ X^β for some β < 0.7784 (ideally β = 1/2 + ε).
Formalization notes: Instead of isomorphism classes of fields we count subfields K of ℂ
(`IntermediateField ℚ ℂ`). An A4-quartic field has trivial automorphism group, so each
isomorphism class corresponds to exactly 4 subfields of ℂ; this changes counts by the constant
factor 4, irrelevant for the exponent. A subfield K is an A4-quartic iff [K:ℚ] = 4 and its normal
closure in ℂ has degree 12 over ℚ (A4 is the only transitive subgroup of S4 of order 12).
The discriminant is Mathlib's `NumberField.discr`; the `NumberField` instance is supplied by an
existential over the (Prop-valued) class, which holds exactly when K is finite-dimensional.
To avoid any junk value from cardinalities of possibly infinite sets, the claim bounds the size
of EVERY finite family of such fields with |Δ| ≤ X (equivalent to bounding N_{A4}(X), which is
finite by Hermite). Proving `Claim` means some exponent β < 0.7784 works for all X ≥ 1 with a
fixed constant C; `¬Claim` means no exponent below 0.7784 works (which would contradict Malle's
conjecture). Known: X^{1/2} log X ≪ N_{A4}(X) ≪ X^{0.7784...+ε}; every β strictly below 0.7784 is a
strict improvement on the record exponent 0.7784....
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM081

/-- `K ⊆ ℂ` is a quartic field with Galois group `A4` and `|disc K| ≤ X`. -/
def IsA4QuarticUpTo (X : ℝ) (K : IntermediateField ℚ ℂ) : Prop :=
  ∃ h : NumberField K,
    Module.finrank ℚ K = 4 ∧
    -- the Galois closure of K (smallest normal subfield of ℂ containing K) has degree 12,
    -- which for a quartic field means Galois group A4
    (∃ M : IntermediateField ℚ ℂ, K ≤ M ∧ Normal ℚ M ∧ Module.finrank ℚ M = 12 ∧
      ∀ M' : IntermediateField ℚ ℂ, K ≤ M' → Normal ℚ M' → M ≤ M') ∧
    |((@NumberField.discr K _ h : ℤ) : ℝ)| ≤ X

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ β : ℝ, β < (0.7784 : ℝ) ∧ ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ X : ℝ, 1 ≤ X →
    ∀ S : Finset (IntermediateField ℚ ℂ), (∀ K ∈ S, IsA4QuarticUpTo X K) →
      (S.card : ℝ) ≤ C * X ^ β

end OpenProblems.QEDM081
prov_reason: Lowering the A4-quartic upper-bound exponent is the standard open target left by BSTTTZ (Thm 1.4) and cited as the record by Loughran-Paterson.

title: Lower the exponent 1/2 in Pasten's subexponential abc bound
credit: Extends H. Pasten, Invent. Math. 2024 (arXiv:2312.03566), Thm 1.4.

math: For coprime $a+b=c$ with $R=\mathrm{rad}(abc)$, Pasten (Invent. Math. 2024, Thm 1.4) proves: if $a\le c^{1-\eta}$ then $\log c\le \eta^{-1}\exp\big(\kappa\sqrt{\log R\,\log_2 R}\big)$; and $\log c\le q\exp(\kappa\sqrt{\log R\log_2R})$ with $q=\min\{P(a),P(b),P(c)\}$. import Mathlib
/-! QED-M082: Lower the exponent 1/2 in Pasten's subexponential abc bound
For coprime a + b = c with R = rad(abc), Pasten (Invent. Math. 2024) proved subexponential
bounds of the shape log c ≤ η⁻¹ exp(κ √(log R · log log R)) (when a ≤ c^{1−η}) and
log c ≤ q exp(κ √(log R · log log R)) with q the smallest of the largest prime factors of a, b, c.
Replace the square root by a smaller power of log R.
Informal statement: Prove, for some fixed θ < 1/2, either: (1) there is κ > 0 such that for all
η ∈ (0,1) and coprime positive a + b = c with a ≤ c^{1−η}, log c ≤ η⁻¹ exp(κ (log R)^θ); or
(2) there is κ > 0 such that for all coprime positive a + b = c,
log c ≤ q · exp(κ (log R)^θ), q = min{P(a), P(b), P(c)}. (The weaker fallback
exp(O(√log R)) is not part of the Claim.)
Formalization notes: rad(n) = ∏ of the distinct primes dividing n (`Nat.primeFactors`);
P(n) = largest prime factor with P(1) = 1, written max 1 (sup of primeFactors). For a coprime
positive triple c ≥ 2, so R ≥ 2 and log R > 0: no junk values in `Real.log` or `rpow`. θ is
required to satisfy 0 < θ < 1/2 (θ ≤ 0 versions are false anyway). The constant κ may depend on θ
only; small-R cases are absorbed by κ since each R admits finitely many triples. Proving `Claim`
= an improvement of Pasten's exponent in either form; `¬Claim` would show that neither form holds
for any θ < 1/2, which would contradict the abc conjecture (abc implies both forms for all θ > 0),
so `¬Claim` is not expected.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM082

/-- Radical: product of the distinct primes dividing `n`. -/
def rad (n : ℕ) : ℕ := ∏ p ∈ n.primeFactors, p

/-- Largest prime factor of `n`, with the convention `P(0) = P(1) = 1`. -/
def gpf (n : ℕ) : ℕ := max 1 (n.primeFactors.sup id)

/-- `(a, b, c)` is a coprime triple of positive integers with `a + b = c`. -/
def IsABC (a b c : ℕ) : Prop := 0 < a ∧ 0 < b ∧ a + b = c ∧ Nat.Coprime a b

/-- Form (1) of the bound with exponent `θ`. -/
def BoundEta (θ : ℝ) : Prop :=

title: Push the GRH lower bound for Montgomery's F(alpha) beyond alpha = 1
credit: Goldston, Gonek, Özlük, Snyder (2000), 'On the pair correlation of zeros of the Riemann zeta-function', Proc. London Math. Soc.
plain: Montgomery's function F(α) is known only for |α|≤1 (on RH). Under GRH for Dirichlet L-functions, Goldston–Gonek–Özlük–Snyder proved F(α) ≥ 3/2−|α|−ε on 1≤|α|≤3/2, while the conjecture says F(α)=1 there. Improve this lower bound.
math: Assume GRH for all Dirichlet $L$-functions. Prove that for some $\delta>0$ and all $\alpha\in[1,1+\delta]$, $\liminf_{T\to\infty}F(\alpha,T)\ge \tfrac32-\alpha+\delta$, or prove $\liminf_T \int_{1}^{3/2}F(\alpha,T)\,d\alpha>1/8$ (the value forced by the GGOS bound).

import Mathlib
/-! QED-M084: Push the GRH lower bound for Montgomery's F(alpha) beyond alpha = 1
Montgomery's pair-correlation function F(α) is known only for |α| ≤ 1 (on RH). Under GRH for Dirichlet L-functions,
Goldston–Gonek–Özlük–Snyder proved F(α) ≥ 3/2 − |α| − ε on 1 ≤ |α| ≤ 3/2, while the conjecture says F(α) = 1 there.
Improve this lower bound.
Informal statement: Assume GRH for all Dirichlet L-functions. Prove that for some δ > 0 and all α ∈ [1, 1+δ],
liminf_{T→∞} F(α,T) ≥ 3/2 − α + δ, or prove liminf_T ∫_1^{3/2} F(α,T) dα > 1/8 (the value forced by the GGOS bound).
Formalization notes: Montgomery's normalization: F(α,T) = (T/(2π) · log T)⁻¹ Σ_{0<γ,γ'≤T} T^{iα(γ−γ')} w(γ−γ'),
w(u) = 4/(4+u²), the sum over ordinates of zeros of ζ on the critical line counted with multiplicity; the sum is real
and equals the cosine form used here. Multiplicity of a zero ρ is the least k with ζ^{(k)}(ρ) ≠ 0 (`zetaOrder`;
it is 0 at non-zeros, so summing over all real γ with weight `mult` is a finite sum, written with `finsum`). Under
GRH (which includes RH via the trivial character mod 1) every nontrivial zero is of the form 1/2 + iγ, so this sum
runs over all nontrivial zeros. GRH is stated for all Dirichlet characters mod q ≥ 1 (Mathlib's `LFunction`, the
completed analytic continuation) in the open strip 0 < Re s < 1; imprimitive characters only add zeros on Re s = 0,
which are excluded. liminf statements are written with explicit ε, T₀. Claim is the implication GRH → (target 1 ∨
target 2), matching the "or" in the problem. Note: ¬Claim would require proving GRH, so only the positive direction
is realistic; this is inherent to a conditional problem.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM084

/-- The Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for all Dirichlet `L`-functions. -/
def GRH : Prop :=
  ∀ (q : ℕ) (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ (q + 1)) (s : ℂ),
    DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s = 0 → 0 < s.re → s.re < 1 → s.re = 1 / 2

/-- Order of vanishing of `ζ` at `s` (`0` if `ζ s ≠ 0`). -/
noncomputable def zetaOrder (s : ℂ) : ℕ := sInf {k : ℕ | iteratedDeriv k riemannZeta s ≠ 0}

/-- Multiplicity of `1/2 + iγ` as a zero of `ζ`, restricted to `0 < γ ≤ T`. -/
noncomputable def mult (T γ : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  if 0 < γ ∧ γ ≤ T then (zetaOrder ((1 / 2 : ℂ) + (γ : ℂ) * Complex.I) : ℝ) else 0

/-- Montgomery's weight. -/
noncomputable def w (u : ℝ) : ℝ := 4 / (4 + u ^ 2)

/-- Montgomery's pair-correlation function `F(α, T)`. -/
noncomputable def F (α T : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  (T / (2 * Real.pi) * Real.log T)⁻¹ *
    ∑ᶠ γ : ℝ, ∑ᶠ γ' : ℝ,
      mult T γ * mult T γ' * Real.cos (α * (γ - γ') * Real.log T) * w (γ - γ')

def Claim : Prop :=
  GRH →
    ((∃ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ ∧ ∀ α ∈ Set.Icc (1 : ℝ) (1 + δ), ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε →
        ∃ T₀ : ℝ, ∀ T : ℝ, T₀ ≤ T → 3 / 2 - α + δ - ε ≤ F α T) ∨
     (∃ c : ℝ, 1 / 8 < c ∧ ∃ T₀ : ℝ, ∀ T : ℝ, T₀ ≤ T →
        c ≤ intervalIntegral (fun α : ℝ => F α T) 1 (3 / 2) MeasureTheory.volume))

end OpenProblems.QEDM084
prov_reason: Asks for a strict improvement of the Goldston–Gonek–Özlük–Snyder GRH lower bound for F(α) on [1, 3/2]; the refs do not pose this improvement explicitly.

title: Second moment of 3-torsion in imaginary quadratic class groups
credit: Cohen, Lenstra, 'Heuristics on class groups of number fields', LNM 1068 (1984); Davenport-Heilbronn (1971) for the first moment
plain: Davenport–Heilbronn showed the average of |Cl(K)[3]| over imaginary quadratic fields is 2, as Cohen–Lenstra predicts. Cohen–Lenstra also predict the average of |Cl(K)[3]|² is 6. Prove this, or at least that the average is bounded.
math: Let $K$ range over imaginary quadratic fields with $|D_K|<X$. Cohen–Lenstra ($\mathbb E\,\#\mathrm{Sur}(\mathrm{Cl}_K,H)=1$ for $H=(\mathbb Z/3)^2$) predict $\frac{1}{\#\{K\}}\sum_K|\mathrm{Cl}_K[3]|^2\to 6$. Prove this limit, or prove $\sum_K|\mathrm{Cl}_K[3]|^2\ll X$.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-M085: Second moment of 3-torsion in imaginary quadratic class groups
Davenport-Heilbronn showed that the average of |Cl(K)[3]| over imaginary quadratic fields K is 2,
as Cohen-Lenstra predict. Cohen-Lenstra also predict that the average of |Cl(K)[3]|² is 6.
Prove this.
Informal statement: Let K range over imaginary quadratic fields with |D_K| < X. Cohen-Lenstra
(E #Sur(Cl_K, H) = 1 for H = (ℤ/3)²) predict (1/#{K}) Σ_K |Cl_K[3]|² → 6 as X → ∞. Prove this
limit. (Fallback, not formalized here: Σ_K |Cl_K[3]|² ≪ X.)
Formalization notes: Imaginary quadratic fields are represented by subfields K of ℂ
(`IntermediateField ℚ ℂ`) of degree 2 over ℚ that are not contained in ℝ. Each imaginary
quadratic field has exactly one image in ℂ (quadratic fields are normal), so this counts
isomorphism classes exactly once. The discriminant is `NumberField.discr`, with the
(Prop-valued) `NumberField` instance supplied existentially; it exists exactly for
finite-dimensional K. `tors3 K` is the number of elements c of the class group of the ring of
integers with c³ = 1, i.e. |Cl_K[3]| (the class group is finite, so `Nat.card` is faithful).
`fieldsUpTo X` is finite for each X (Hermite), so `Set.ncard` and `finsum` are faithful; for
small X the average is 0/0 = 0 in Lean, which does not affect the limit. Proving `Claim` proves
the Cohen-Lenstra second-moment prediction (average → 6); proving `¬Claim` disproves it.
Identity behind 6: |Cl[3]|² = #Hom(Cl, (ℤ/3)²) = Σ_{H ≤ (ℤ/3)²} #Sur(Cl, H), with 1 + 4 + 1 subgroups.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM085

/-- `K ⊆ ℂ` is an imaginary quadratic field with `|disc K| < X`. -/
def IsImagQuadUpTo (X : ℝ) (K : IntermediateField ℚ ℂ) : Prop :=
  ∃ h : NumberField K,
    Module.finrank ℚ K = 2 ∧
    (∃ x : K, (x : ℂ).im ≠ 0) ∧
    |((@NumberField.discr K _ h : ℤ) : ℝ)| < X

/-- The (finite) set of imaginary quadratic subfields of `ℂ` with `|disc| < X`. -/
def fieldsUpTo (X : ℝ) : Set (IntermediateField ℚ ℂ) :=
  {K : IntermediateField ℚ ℂ | IsImagQuadUpTo X K}

/-- `|Cl_K[3]|`: the number of ideal classes of `𝓞_K` whose cube is trivial. -/
noncomputable def tors3 (K : IntermediateField ℚ ℂ) : ℕ :=
  Nat.card {c : ClassGroup (NumberField.RingOfIntegers K) // c ^ 3 = 1}

/-- Average of `|Cl_K[3]|²` over imaginary quadratic fields with `|disc| < X`. -/
noncomputable def secondMoment (X : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  (∑ᶠ K ∈ fieldsUpTo X, ((tors3 K : ℝ) ^ 2)) / ((fieldsUpTo X).ncard : ℝ)

def Claim : Prop :=
  Filter.Tendsto secondMoment Filter.atTop (nhds (6 : ℝ))

end OpenProblems.QEDM085
prov_reason: The average 6 for |Cl[3]|² over imaginary quadratic fields is a direct Cohen-Lenstra prediction and a well-known open case beyond Davenport-Heilbronn.

title: A Jörgens theorem for the Hessian permanent
plain: Jörgens proved that a convex function on the whole plane whose Hessian determinant is 1 must be a quadratic polynomial. Replace the determinant by the permanent, u_xx·u_yy + u_xy², and ask whether the same rigidity holds for solutions on the elliptic branch.
math: Let $u\in C^4(\mathbb R^2)$ satisfy $u_{xx}u_{yy}+u_{xy}^2=1$, $u_{xx}>0$ and $2u_{xy}^2<1$ on $\mathbb R^2$ (these are exactly the conditions for the linearized operator $u_{yy}\partial_{xx}+2u_{xy}\partial_{xy}+u_{xx}\partial_{yy}$ to be elliptic; they force $u$ convex with $0<\det D^2u=1-2u_{xy}^2\le1$). Prove or disprove that $u$ is a quadratic polynomial.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-M086: A Jörgens theorem for the Hessian permanent
Jörgens proved that a convex entire solution of det D^2 u = 1 in the plane is a quadratic
polynomial. Replace the determinant by the permanent u_xx u_yy + u_xy^2 and ask whether entire
solutions on the elliptic branch are still quadratic.
Informal statement: Let u ∈ C^4(R^2) satisfy u_xx u_yy + u_xy^2 = 1, u_xx > 0 and 2 u_xy^2 < 1
on R^2. Prove or disprove that u is a quadratic polynomial.
Formalization notes: u : ℝ × ℝ → ℝ with `ContDiff ℝ 4 u`. Second partials are values of the
second Fréchet derivative: u_xx = D^2u(p)(e1,e1), u_xy = D^2u(p)(e1,e2), u_yy = D^2u(p)(e2,e2)
with e1 = (1,0), e2 = (0,1). The conditions u_xx > 0 and 2u_xy^2 < 1 are exactly ellipticity of
the linearized operator; they imply convexity. "Quadratic polynomial" means
u(x,y) = a x^2 + b xy + c y^2 + d x + e y + f for real constants (any degree <= 2 polynomial).
Quadratic solutions exist (e.g. (x^2+y^2)/2), so the hypothesis is not vacuous. Proving Claim
is the Jörgens-type rigidity theorem; proving ¬Claim exhibits a non-quadratic entire elliptic
solution.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM086

/-- Second Fréchet derivative of `u` at `p` applied to `(v, w)`. -/
noncomputable def secondPartial (u : ℝ × ℝ → ℝ) (p : ℝ × ℝ) (v w : ℝ × ℝ) : ℝ :=
  fderiv ℝ (fderiv ℝ u) p v w

/-- Unit vector in the x direction. -/
def ex : ℝ × ℝ := (1, 0)

/-- Unit vector in the y direction. -/
def ey : ℝ × ℝ := (0, 1)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ u : ℝ × ℝ → ℝ, ContDiff ℝ 4 u →
    (∀ p : ℝ × ℝ,
      secondPartial u p ex ex * secondPartial u p ey ey + secondPartial u p ex ey ^ 2 = 1 ∧
      0 < secondPartial u p ex ex ∧
      2 * secondPartial u p ex ey ^ 2 < 1) →
    ∃ a b c d e f : ℝ, ∀ x y : ℝ,
      u (x, y) = a * x ^ 2 + b * x * y + c * y ^ 2 + d * x + e * y + f

end OpenProblems.QEDM086
prov_reason: Notes report no literature on the permanent equation u_xx u_yy + u_xy^2 = 1; the Jörgens-type question for it was formulated by QED.

import Mathlib
/-! QED-M087: Blow-up under a steady force
Can a smooth, compactly supported, time-independent force drive the incompressible Navier–Stokes
fluid on ℝ³, starting at rest, to a finite-time singularity?
Informal statement: Decide whether there is f ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ³;ℝ³), independent of t, such that the solution
of ∂_t u + (u·∇)u + ∇p = Δu + f, ∇·u = 0, u(·,0) = 0 on ℝ³ loses smoothness in finite time.
(Claim: such an f exists.)
Formalization notes: Following the Clay formulation, "loses smoothness in finite time" means there is
no global smooth solution: no pair (u, P) smooth on ℝ³ × [0,∞) (`ContDiffOn ℝ n` on {t ≥ 0} for every
n) with u(x,0) = 0, satisfying the equations pointwise for t > 0, with locally-in-time bounded energy
∫|u(x,t)|² dx (a steady force can make energy grow, so a uniform-in-time bound as in Clay's (A)/(B)
would be wrong here; the lintegral avoids Bochner-integral junk values). Smooth finite-energy
solutions are unique, so this matches blow-up of the unique local smooth solution. Gradient forces
are trivially excluded (u = 0, P = potential).
Proving `Claim` = exhibiting a steady C_c^∞ force with finite-time blow-up. Proving `¬Claim` = global
regularity from rest for every steady C_c^∞ force.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM087

/-- ℝ³. -/
abbrev R3 : Type := Fin 3 → ℝ

/-- Space-time ℝ³ × ℝ. -/
abbrev ST : Type := R3 × ℝ

/-- Spatial partial derivative ∂_j of a scalar field. -/
noncomputable def dx (j : Fin 3) (g : ST → ℝ) (z : ST) : ℝ :=
  fderiv ℝ g z ((Pi.single j (1 : ℝ) : R3), (0 : ℝ))

/-- Time derivative of a scalar field. -/
noncomputable def dtt (g : ST → ℝ) (z : ST) : ℝ := fderiv ℝ g z ((0 : R3), (1 : ℝ))

/-- `(u, P)` is a global smooth locally-finite-energy solution from rest with steady force `f`. -/
def IsGlobalSmoothSolution (f : R3 → R3) (u : ST → R3) (P : ST → ℝ) : Prop :=
  (∀ n : ℕ, ContDiffOn ℝ n u {z : ST | 0 ≤ z.2}) ∧
  (∀ n : ℕ, ContDiffOn ℝ n P {z : ST | 0 ≤ z.2}) ∧
  (∀ x : R3, u (x, 0) = 0) ∧
  (∀ z : ST, 0 < z.2 → ∀ i : Fin 3,
    dtt (fun w => u w i) z + ∑ j : Fin 3, u z j * dx j (fun w => u w i) z + dx i P z =
      ∑ j : Fin 3, dx j (fun w => dx j (fun w' => u w' i) w) z + f z.1 i) ∧
  (∀ z : ST, 0 < z.2 → ∑ j : Fin 3, dx j (fun w => u w j) z = 0) ∧
  (∀ T : ℝ, ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ t : ℝ, 0 ≤ t → t ≤ T →
    ∫⁻ x : R3, ENNReal.ofReal (∑ i : Fin 3, (u (x, t) i) ^ 2) ≤ ENNReal.ofReal C)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ f : R3 → R3, (∀ n : ℕ, ContDiff ℝ n f) ∧ HasCompactSupport f ∧
    ¬ ∃ (u : ST → R3) (P : ST → ℝ), IsGlobalSmoothSolution f u P

end OpenProblems.QEDM087
prov_reason: This is a time-independent-force strengthening of the forced (Clay-type, OpenAI-claimed) Navier-Stokes blow-up.

title: Critical NLS blow-up threshold on the cube surface
credit: Extension of Weinstein (Comm. Math. Phys. 1983) mass-critical threshold; related Strichartz work on flat cones by Ford and by Blair-Ford-Marzuola.
plain: In the plane, the focusing cubic Schrödinger equation needs at least the ground-state mass to blow up. On the surface of a cube, each corner is a cone with total angle 3π/2, which can hold a 'three-quarter' ground state. So the blow-up threshold should drop to three quarters of the planar one, and the claim is that it does exactly that.
math: Let $S$ be the surface of the unit cube with its flat metric, and let $\Delta$ be the Friedrichs extension of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on $C_c^\infty(S\setminus\{\text{vertices}\})$. Let $Q$ be the ground state of $\Delta Q-Q+Q^3=0$ on $\mathbb R^2$, and put $m_*=\tfrac34\|Q\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}^2$. For $iu_t+\Delta u+|u|^2u=0$ on $S$, prove: (i) every $u_0\in H^1(S)$ with $\|u_0\|_2^2<m_*$ gives a global $H^1$ solution; (ii) for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $u_0\in H^1(S)$ with $m_*<\|u_0\|_2^2<m_*+\varepsilon$ whose solution blows up in finite time. (Stronger, optional: blow-up data exist for every mass $m>m_*$; also decide whether there is blow-up at mass exactly $m_*$.)

title: Does an oscillating source lower the Strauss exponent?
results: Bound p_c<=1+sqrt2 is correct: John/Zhou iteration uses only |F(u)|<=C|u|^p and |F(u)-F(v)|<=C(|u|+|v|)^{p-1}|u-v|, both hold for g(t)|u|^p. The 'resonance predicts 2' heuristic (exp of int t^{1-p}) is arithmetically right but not an argument; a normal-form attempt (H''=g) just recycles the oscillating factor, so nothing is proved.

plain: For the 3D wave equation with source |u|^p, small smooth data give global solutions exactly when p > 1+√2 (Strauss). Multiply the source by a factor that oscillates periodically in time with average zero, such as cos t. The global-existence proof still works above 1+√2. Every blow-up proof below it breaks, because they all need the source to be positive. Is the true threshold strictly smaller?
math: Let $g$ be smooth, $2\pi$-periodic, $\int_0^{2\pi}g=0$, $g\not\equiv0$ (model $g=\cos t$). For $u_{tt}-\Delta u=g(t)|u|^p$ on $\mathbb R^{1+3}$ with data $\varepsilon(f,h)$, $f,h\in C_c^\infty$ (solutions in the usual weak/mild sense, e.g. $C([0,T);H^1)$ with John-type weighted bounds), let $p_c(g)=\inf\{p>1:\forall f,h\ \exists\varepsilon_0>0$ such that the solution is global for all $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0\}$. Since John/Zhou/Glassey global existence uses only $|g|u|^p|\lesssim|u|^p$ and the matching Lipschitz bound, $p_c(g)\le1+\sqrt2$. Is $p_c(g)<1+\sqrt2$? Determine $p_c(g)$ and whether it depends on $g$ (a heuristic predicts 2). For $1<p<p_c(g)$, determine the lifespan $T_\varepsilon$ as $\varepsilon\to0$ for suitable data.

import Mathlib
/-! QED-M091: Euler with reversed stretching
Flip the sign of the vortex-stretching term in the 3D Euler vorticity equation on the torus, keeping advection and the
Biot–Savart law. Do smooth solutions stay smooth forever, or can they blow up in finite time?
Informal statement: On 𝕋³ let ω : 𝕋³ × [0,T) → ℝ³ solve ∂ₜω + (u·∇)ω = −Sω, where u = ∇ × (−Δ)⁻¹(ω − ⟨ω⟩),
S = ½(∇u + ∇uᵀ) and ⟨ω⟩ is the spatial mean. Decide whether every ω₀ ∈ C^∞(𝕋³; ℝ³) with ∇·ω₀ = 0 generates a global
smooth solution.
Formalization notes: 𝕋³ = (ℝ/2πℤ)³ is encoded by 2π-periodic functions on ℝ³ = (Fin 3 → ℝ). Spatial partial derivatives
are Fréchet derivatives in coordinate directions (`pd i F x = ∂ᵢF(x)`), the time derivative is `deriv`. The spatial mean is
(2π)⁻³ times the Bochner integral over the cell [0,2π]³. The Biot–Savart velocity is u = curl ψ where ψ is the
mean-zero periodic solution of Δψ = −(ω − ⟨ω⟩) (unique; ψ is required to exist as part of the solution, and its
joint smoothness is automatic for smooth ω, so requiring it loses nothing). We do NOT assume div ω = 0 for t > 0
(the reversed equation does not preserve it), which is why u is defined through ψ rather than by curl u = ω.
(Sω)ᵢ = Σⱼ ½(∂ⱼuᵢ + ∂ᵢuⱼ)ωⱼ. Smoothness is "C^k for every k ∈ ℕ" jointly in (t,x) on ℝ × ℝ³; since any smooth function on
[0,∞) × ℝ³ extends smoothly to t < 0, this is the same as smoothness on [0,∞) × 𝕋³. The equation is imposed for t > 0
(it then holds at t = 0 by continuity). Smooth solutions are unique, so existence of a global smooth solution is
the same as absence of finite-time blow-up. Proving Claim = global regularity for all smooth divergence-free data;
proving ¬Claim = some smooth periodic divergence-free ω₀ with no global smooth solution (finite-time blow-up).
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM091

/-- Partial derivative `∂ᵢ F (x)` of a vector field `F : ℝ³ → ℝ³`. -/
noncomputable def pd (i : Fin 3) (F : (Fin 3 → ℝ) → (Fin 3 → ℝ)) (x : Fin 3 → ℝ) : Fin 3 → ℝ :=
  fderiv ℝ F x (Pi.single i 1)

/-- Vector Laplacian. -/
noncomputable def lap (F : (Fin 3 → ℝ) → (Fin 3 → ℝ)) (x : Fin 3 → ℝ) : Fin 3 → ℝ :=
  ∑ i : Fin 3, pd i (pd i F) x

/-- Curl `∇ × F`. -/
noncomputable def curl (F : (Fin 3 → ℝ) → (Fin 3 → ℝ)) (x : Fin 3 → ℝ) : Fin 3 → ℝ :=
  ![pd 1 F x 2 - pd 2 F x 1, pd 2 F x 0 - pd 0 F x 2, pd 0 F x 1 - pd 1 F x 0]

/-- Divergence `∇ · F`. -/
noncomputable def divg (F : (Fin 3 → ℝ) → (Fin 3 → ℝ)) (x : Fin 3 → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∑ i : Fin 3, pd i F x i

/-- `F` is `2π`-periodic in each coordinate (a field on `𝕋³`). -/
def IsPeriodic (F : (Fin 3 → ℝ) → (Fin 3 → ℝ)) : Prop :=
  ∀ (x : Fin 3 → ℝ) (i : Fin 3), F (x + Pi.single i (2 * Real.pi)) = F x

/-- The fundamental cell `[0, 2π]³`. -/
noncomputable def cell : Set (Fin 3 → ℝ) := Set.Icc (0 : Fin 3 → ℝ) (fun _ => 2 * Real.pi)

/-- Spatial mean over the torus. -/
noncomputable def mean (F : (Fin 3 → ℝ) → (Fin 3 → ℝ)) : Fin 3 → ℝ :=
  (1 / (2 * Real.pi) ^ 3) • MeasureTheory.integral (MeasureTheory.volume.restrict cell) F

/-- `(S ω)ᵢ = Σⱼ ½ (∂ⱼ uᵢ + ∂ᵢ uⱼ) ωⱼ` with `S` the symmetric gradient of `u` at `x`. -/
noncomputable def strainApply (u : (Fin 3 → ℝ) → (Fin 3 → ℝ)) (w : Fin 3 → ℝ) (x : Fin 3 → ℝ) : Fin 3 → ℝ :=
  fun i => ∑ j : Fin 3, (1 / 2 : ℝ) * (pd j u x i + pd i u x j) * w j

/-- Joint smoothness in `(t, x)`: `C^k` for every `k`. -/
def IsSmoothTX (f : ℝ → (Fin 3 → ℝ) → (Fin 3 → ℝ)) : Prop :=
  ∀ k : ℕ, ContDiff ℝ k (fun p : ℝ × (Fin 3 → ℝ) => f p.1 p.2)

/-- `(ω, ψ)` is a global smooth solution with initial vorticity `ω₀`; the velocity is `u(t) = curl ψ(t)`. -/
def IsGlobalSolution (ω₀ : (Fin 3 → ℝ) → (Fin 3 → ℝ)) (ω ψ : ℝ → (Fin 3 → ℝ) → (Fin 3 → ℝ)) : Prop :=
  IsSmoothTX ω ∧ IsSmoothTX ψ ∧ ω 0 = ω₀ ∧
  (∀ t : ℝ, 0 ≤ t →
    IsPeriodic (ω t) ∧ IsPeriodic (ψ t) ∧ mean (ψ t) = 0 ∧
    ∀ x : Fin 3 → ℝ, lap (ψ t) x = -(ω t x - mean (ω t))) ∧
  (∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → ∀ x : Fin 3 → ℝ,
    deriv (fun s : ℝ => ω s x) t + ∑ j : Fin 3, (curl (ψ t) x j) • pd j (ω t) x
      = -(strainApply (curl (ψ t)) (ω t x) x))

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ ω₀ : (Fin 3 → ℝ) → (Fin 3 → ℝ),
    (∀ k : ℕ, ContDiff ℝ k ω₀) → IsPeriodic ω₀ → (∀ x, divg ω₀ x = 0) →
      ∃ ω ψ : ℝ → (Fin 3 → ℝ) → (Fin 3 → ℝ), IsGlobalSolution ω₀ ω ψ

end OpenProblems.QEDM091
prov_reason: No source poses the 3D Euler model with reversed vortex stretching; only 1D analogues (De Gregorio, Córdoba–Córdoba–Fontelos, Okamoto–Sakajo–Wunsch, Elgindi–Jeong) study the sign of stretching.

import Mathlib
/-! QED-M093: Forced Navier–Stokes blow-up at a no-slip wall
In 2026 it was shown that a smooth, compactly supported force can drive the 3D Navier–Stokes
equations, started from rest, to blow up in finite time, but the construction is interior.
Show that blow-up can happen at the wall itself: in the half-space {x₃ > 0} with the no-slip
condition, a smooth finite-energy solution started from rest and driven by a smooth compactly
supported force becomes unbounded in finite time, while staying bounded away from the wall.
Informal statement: Let ℝ³₊ = {x₃ > 0}, ν > 0. Construct f ∈ C_c^∞(closure(ℝ³₊) × (0,∞); ℝ³) and a
solution (u,p) of ∂ₜu − νΔu + (u·∇)u + ∇p = f, ∇·u = 0 in ℝ³₊ × (0,T), u = 0 on {x₃ = 0},
u(·,0) = 0, with u ∈ C^∞(closure(ℝ³₊) × [0,T)), sup_{t<T} ‖u(t)‖_{L²} < ∞ and
limsup_{t↑T} ‖u(t)‖_{L^∞} = ∞, such that u stays bounded on {x₃ > r} × [0,T) for every r > 0
(all singular points lie on the wall).
Formalization notes: Space is `Fin 3 → ℝ`; coordinate `x 2` is the wall-normal x₃. Derivatives
are Fréchet derivatives (`fderiv`, `deriv`), so the norm on `Fin 3 → ℝ` is irrelevant; the
squared Euclidean length is written out as `sqNorm`. Smoothness up to the boundary on
closure(ℝ³₊) × [0,T) is encoded as: u and p are restrictions of functions that are C^k for every
k on the open set ℝ³ × (−∞,T) (equivalent by Seeley/Whitney extension); values with x₃ < 0 or
t < 0 are irrelevant. The force is C^k for all k on ℝ³ × ℝ and vanishes outside a box
{|xᵢ| ≤ R, δ ≤ t ≤ R} with δ > 0 (compact support in closure(ℝ³₊) × (0,∞)). Two side conditions
make "the singular points lie on (a bounded part of) the wall" precise and rule out cheap
solutions: (i) u is bounded on {x₃ ≥ 0, max(|x₁|,|x₂|) > R₀} × [0,T) (no escape to horizontal
infinity), and (ii) for each t < T the pressure p(·,t) is bounded on the closed half-space (this
excludes harmonic, e.g. linear, pressures acting as a hidden non-decaying force). Together with
boundedness on {x₃ > r} and smoothness on [0,T), unboundedness can only come from points of a
compact piece of the wall as t ↑ T. The energy condition requires x ↦ |u(x,t)|² integrable on
ℝ³₊ with uniformly bounded integral. Proving `Claim` = constructing such a blow-up for every
ν > 0; proving `¬Claim` = showing that for some ν > 0 no such boundary blow-up exists.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM093

open MeasureTheory

/-- Points of ℝ³; the coordinate `x 2` is the wall-normal coordinate x₃. -/
abbrev R3 : Type := Fin 3 → ℝ

/-- Squared Euclidean length of a vector in ℝ³. -/
def sqNorm (v : R3) : ℝ := ∑ i : Fin 3, v i ^ 2

/-- Standard basis vector `eᵢ`. -/
def basisVec (i : Fin 3) : R3 := Pi.single i (1 : ℝ)

/-- Spatial partial derivative `∂ᵢ u (x,t)` of a time-dependent vector field. -/
noncomputable def dx (u : R3 → ℝ → R3) (i : Fin 3) (x : R3) (t : ℝ) : R3 :=
  fderiv ℝ (fun y : R3 => u y t) x (basisVec i)

/-- Spatial Laplacian `Δu (x,t) = ∑ᵢ ∂ᵢ∂ᵢ u`. -/
noncomputable def lap (u : R3 → ℝ → R3) (x : R3) (t : ℝ) : R3 :=
  ∑ i : Fin 3, dx (fun y s => dx u i y s) i x t

/-- Time derivative `∂ₜ u (x,t)`. -/
noncomputable def dt (u : R3 → ℝ → R3) (x : R3) (t : ℝ) : R3 :=
  deriv (fun s : ℝ => u x s) t

/-- Convective term `(u·∇)u (x,t) = ∑ⱼ uⱼ ∂ⱼ u`. -/
noncomputable def convec (u : R3 → ℝ → R3) (x : R3) (t : ℝ) : R3 :=
  ∑ j : Fin 3, (u x t j) • dx u j x t

/-- Spatial gradient of a scalar field. -/
noncomputable def grad (p : R3 → ℝ → ℝ) (x : R3) (t : ℝ) : R3 :=
  fun i => fderiv ℝ (fun y : R3 => p y t) x (basisVec i)

/-- Divergence `∇·u (x,t)`. -/
noncomputable def divg (u : R3 → ℝ → R3) (x : R3) (t : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∑ i : Fin 3, dx u i x t i

/-- The open half-space `{x₃ > 0}`. -/
def halfSpace : Set R3 := {x : R3 | 0 < x 2}

/-- `(f,u,p,T)` is a boundary blow-up solution of forced Navier–Stokes with viscosity `ν`
in the half-space with no-slip condition, as described in the header. -/
def BoundaryBlowup (ν T : ℝ) (f u : R3 → ℝ → R3) (p : R3 → ℝ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  0 < T ∧
  -- smooth force with compact support in closure(ℝ³₊) × (0, ∞)
  (∀ k : ℕ, ContDiff ℝ k (fun q : R3 × ℝ => f q.1 q.2)) ∧
  (∃ R δ : ℝ, 0 < δ ∧ ∀ (x : R3) (t : ℝ), f x t ≠ 0 →
      (δ ≤ t ∧ t ≤ R ∧ ∀ i : Fin 3, |x i| ≤ R)) ∧
  -- smoothness of u and p up to the wall and up to (but excluding) time T
  (∀ k : ℕ, ContDiffOn ℝ k (fun q : R3 × ℝ => u q.1 q.2) (Set.univ ×ˢ Set.Iio T)) ∧
  (∀ k : ℕ, ContDiffOn ℝ k (fun q : R3 × ℝ => p q.1 q.2) (Set.univ ×ˢ Set.Iio T)) ∧
  -- the equations in ℝ³₊ × (0,T)
  (∀ (x : R3) (t : ℝ), 0 < x 2 → 0 < t → t < T →
      dt u x t - ν • lap u x t + convec u x t + grad p x t = f x t) ∧
  (∀ (x : R3) (t : ℝ), 0 < x 2 → 0 < t → t < T → divg u x t = 0) ∧
  -- no-slip and initial condition
  (∀ (x : R3) (t : ℝ), x 2 = 0 → 0 ≤ t → t < T → u x t = 0) ∧
  (∀ x : R3, 0 ≤ x 2 → u x 0 = 0) ∧
  -- finite energy, uniformly in time
  (∃ C : ℝ, ∀ t : ℝ, 0 ≤ t → t < T →
      IntegrableOn (fun x : R3 => sqNorm (u x t)) halfSpace ∧
      ∫ x in halfSpace, sqNorm (u x t) ≤ C) ∧
  -- pressure bounded at each time (excludes harmonic pressures)
  (∀ t : ℝ, 0 ≤ t → t < T → ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ x : R3, 0 ≤ x 2 → |p x t| ≤ C) ∧
  -- blow-up: u is unbounded on closure(ℝ³₊) × [0,T)
  (∀ M : ℝ, ∃ (x : R3) (t : ℝ), 0 ≤ x 2 ∧ 0 ≤ t ∧ t < T ∧ M < sqNorm (u x t)) ∧
  -- bounded away from the wall
  (∀ r : ℝ, 0 < r → ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ (x : R3) (t : ℝ), r < x 2 → 0 ≤ t → t < T →
      sqNorm (u x t) ≤ C) ∧
  -- bounded far out along the wall (singularities in a compact part of the wall)
  (∃ R₀ C : ℝ, ∀ (x : R3) (t : ℝ), 0 ≤ x 2 → 0 ≤ t → t < T →
      (R₀ < |x 0| ∨ R₀ < |x 1|) → sqNorm (u x t) ≤ C)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ ν : ℝ, 0 < ν →
    ∃ (T : ℝ) (f u : R3 → ℝ → R3) (p : R3 → ℝ → ℝ), BoundaryBlowup ν T f u p

title: Heat with a cosine reaction
credit: H. Fujita 1966 (critical exponent); R. Pinsky 1997 (weighted Fujita problem, a >= 0)
plain: In u_t = u_xx + cos(x) u^2 the reaction term averages to zero over a period, but a second-order (homogenization) effect produces an effective +u^3 term, which in one dimension is exactly Fujita's borderline exponent where every positive solution of u_t = u_xx + u^3 blows up. Does every positive solution of the cosine equation blow up in finite time?
math: Let $d\ge1$, $a\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ be $\mathbb Z^d$-periodic with $\int_{[0,1]^d}a=0$, $a\not\equiv0$. Consider $u_t=\Delta u+a(x)u^p$, $u(\cdot,0)=u_0\in C_c(\mathbb R^d)$, $u_0\ge0$, $u_0\not\equiv0$. Prove: (i) if $1<p\le1+1/d$, every such solution blows up in finite time; (ii) if $p>1+1/d$, solutions with sufficiently small $u_0$ are global. Test case: $d=1$, $p=2$, $a=\cos(2\pi x)$ (equivalently $a=\cos x$ with $2\pi$-periodicity).

import Mathlib
/-! QED-M094: Heat with a cosine reaction
For u_t = Δu + a(x)u^p with a periodic, mean-zero, not identically zero weight, the first-order reaction
averages out, but homogenization produces an effective +c·u^{2p−1} term, predicting the Fujita-type
threshold p* = 1 + 1/d. The test case u_t = u_xx + cos(2πx)u² is exactly critical.
Informal statement: Let d ≥ 1, a ∈ C^∞(ℝ^d) ℤ^d-periodic with ∫_{[0,1]^d} a = 0, a ≢ 0. Consider
u_t = Δu + a(x)u^p, u(·,0) = u₀ ∈ C_c(ℝ^d), u₀ ≥ 0, u₀ ≢ 0. Prove: (i) if 1 < p ≤ 1 + 1/d, every such
solution blows up in finite time; (ii) if p > 1 + 1/d, then for every such u₀ the solution with
initial data εu₀ is global for all sufficiently small ε > 0.
Formalization notes: A global solution is u : ℝ^d × ℝ → ℝ, C² on {t > 0}, continuous on {t ≥ 0},
nonnegative, bounded on every strip ℝ^d × [0,T], with u(x,0) = u₀(x) and u_t = Δu + a u^p pointwise
for t > 0 (partials via `fderiv`; `u^p` is `Real.rpow`, meaningful since u ≥ 0; nonnegativity holds for
the true solution by the comparison principle). By local well-posedness and uniqueness in the class
of solutions bounded on strips, "blows up in finite time" ⇔ "no global solution in this class".
For (ii), "sufficiently small u₀" is read profile-wise (data εu₀, ε small), the standard Fujita form.
Smoothness of a is `∀ n : ℕ, ContDiff ℝ n a`.
Proving `Claim` = both (i) and (ii) for all d, a, p. Proving `¬Claim` = a counterexample to either:
a global positive solution for some p ≤ 1 + 1/d, or a supercritical p and profile u₀ for which
arbitrarily small multiples blow up.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM094

/-- ℝ^d. -/
abbrev Rd (d : ℕ) : Type := Fin d → ℝ

/-- Spatial Laplacian of `u` at `z = (x,t)`. -/
noncomputable def lap {d : ℕ} (u : Rd d × ℝ → ℝ) (z : Rd d × ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∑ i : Fin d,
    fderiv ℝ (fun y : Rd d × ℝ => fderiv ℝ u y ((Pi.single i (1 : ℝ) : Rd d), (0 : ℝ))) z
      ((Pi.single i (1 : ℝ) : Rd d), (0 : ℝ))

/-- Time derivative of `u` at `z`. -/
noncomputable def dt {d : ℕ} (u : Rd d × ℝ → ℝ) (z : Rd d × ℝ) : ℝ :=
  fderiv ℝ u z ((0 : Rd d), (1 : ℝ))

/-- Admissible weight: smooth, ℤ^d-periodic, mean zero, not identically zero. -/
def AdmissibleWeight (d : ℕ) (a : Rd d → ℝ) : Prop :=
  (∀ n : ℕ, ContDiff ℝ n a) ∧
  (∀ (x : Rd d) (i : Fin d), a (x + Pi.single i (1 : ℝ)) = a x) ∧
  (∫ x in Set.Icc (0 : Rd d) 1, a x) = 0 ∧
  (∃ x, a x ≠ 0)

/-- Admissible initial datum: continuous, compactly supported, nonnegative, not identically zero. -/
def AdmissibleDatum (d : ℕ) (u₀ : Rd d → ℝ) : Prop :=
  Continuous u₀ ∧ HasCompactSupport u₀ ∧ (∀ x, 0 ≤ u₀ x) ∧ (∃ x, u₀ x ≠ 0)

/-- `u` is a global (bounded on strips) classical nonnegative solution. -/
def IsGlobalSolution (d : ℕ) (a : Rd d → ℝ) (p : ℝ) (u₀ : Rd d → ℝ) (u : Rd d × ℝ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ContDiffOn ℝ 2 u {z | 0 < z.2} ∧
  ContinuousOn u {z | 0 ≤ z.2} ∧
  (∀ x, u (x, 0) = u₀ x) ∧
  (∀ z : Rd d × ℝ, 0 ≤ z.2 → 0 ≤ u z) ∧
  (∀ T : ℝ, ∃ M : ℝ, ∀ z : Rd d × ℝ, 0 ≤ z.2 → z.2 ≤ T → |u z| ≤ M) ∧
  (∀ z : Rd d × ℝ, 0 < z.2 → dt u z = lap u z + a z.1 * u z ^ p)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ d : ℕ, 1 ≤ d → ∀ a : Rd d → ℝ, AdmissibleWeight d a → ∀ p : ℝ, 1 < p →
    (p ≤ 1 + 1 / (d : ℝ) →
      ∀ u₀ : Rd d → ℝ, AdmissibleDatum d u₀ → ∀ u : Rd d × ℝ → ℝ, ¬ IsGlobalSolution d a p u₀ u) ∧
    (1 + 1 / (d : ℝ) < p →
      ∀ u₀ : Rd d → ℝ, AdmissibleDatum d u₀ → ∃ ε₀ : ℝ, 0 < ε₀ ∧ ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ε < ε₀ →
        ∃ u : Rd d × ℝ → ℝ, IsGlobalSolution d a p (fun x => ε * u₀ x) u)

end OpenProblems.QEDM094
prov_reason: This extends Fujita's blow-up/global threshold to sign-changing, mean-zero periodic weights; the known weighted results (Pinsky and others) assume a >= 0.

title: KdV with a cosine coefficient
plain: Put a cos x in front of the cubic term of the modified KdV equation on the circle. The energy and the mean are still conserved, but the L² norm is not, and the energy no longer has a definite sign. Can smooth solutions blow up in finite time?
math: Consider $u_t+u_{xxx}+(\cos(x)\,u^3)_x=0$ on $\mathbb T=\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$ with real $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb T)$. It is Hamiltonian, $u_t=\partial_x\frac{\delta H}{\delta u}$ with $H=\int(\tfrac12u_x^2-\tfrac14\cos(x)u^4)$, and conserves $\int u$ and $H$. However, $\frac{d}{dt}\int u^2=\frac12\int\sin(x)u^4$. Decide whether every such $u_0$ yields a global smooth solution, or whether $\|u(t)\|_{H^1}\to\infty$ in finite time for some $u_0$.

/-! QED-M095: KdV with a cosine coefficient
Put a cos x in front of the cubic term of the modified KdV equation on the circle. The energy
and the mean are still conserved, but the L² norm is not, and the energy is indefinite. Can
smooth solutions blow up in finite time?
Informal statement: Consider u_t + u_xxx + (cos(x) u³)_x = 0 on 𝕋 = ℝ/2πℤ with real
u₀ ∈ C^∞(𝕋). It is Hamiltonian with H = ∫(½u_x² − ¼cos(x)u⁴), conserves ∫u and H, and
d/dt ∫u² = ½∫ sin(x) u⁴. Decide whether every such u₀ yields a global smooth solution, or
whether ‖u(t)‖_{H¹} → ∞ in finite time for some u₀.
Formalization notes:
* Functions on 𝕋 are 2π-periodic functions on ℝ. A global smooth solution is
  u : ℝ × ℝ → ℝ (time, space), C^n for every n ∈ ℕ (i.e. C^∞; written this way to avoid
  `⊤` meaning analytic), 2π-periodic in x, with u(0,x) = u₀(x) and the equation holding
  pointwise for all t ≥ 0. Requiring u to be smooth on all of ℝ × ℝ (with the equation only
  for t ≥ 0) loses nothing: a C^∞ function on [0,∞) × 𝕋 extends smoothly to t < 0.
* Derivatives are partial derivatives via `deriv` of sections; `iteratedDeriv 3` for u_xxx.

  Proving `¬Claim`: some smooth u₀ has no global smooth solution; by standard local
  well-posedness in H^s (s large) with the blow-up alternative and persistence of regularity,
  this is equivalent to finite-time blow-up of ‖u(t)‖_{H¹} (the H¹ norm controls all higher
  norms for this equation), matching the dichotomy in the informal statement.

namespace OpenProblems.QEDM095

/-- `u` is a global (forward in time) smooth 2π-periodic solution of

def IsGlobalSmoothSolution (u₀ : ℝ → ℝ) (u : ℝ × ℝ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  (∀ n : ℕ, ContDiff ℝ n u) ∧
  (∀ t x : ℝ, u (t, x + 2 * Real.pi) = u (t, x)) ∧
  (∀ x : ℝ, u (0, x) = u₀ x) ∧
  ∀ t : ℝ, 0 ≤ t → ∀ x : ℝ,
    deriv (fun s : ℝ => u (s, x)) t
      + iteratedDeriv 3 (fun y : ℝ => u (t, y)) x
      + deriv (fun y : ℝ => Real.cos y * (u (t, y)) ^ 3) x = 0

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ u₀ : ℝ → ℝ, (∀ n : ℕ, ContDiff ℝ n u₀) → Function.Periodic u₀ (2 * Real.pi) →
    ∃ u : ℝ × ℝ → ℝ, IsGlobalSmoothSolution u₀ u

end OpenProblems.QEDM095

title: Liouville theorem for Lane-Emden with a shifted nonlinearity
plain: Gidas-Spruck: -Delta u = u^p has no positive solution on R^n for subcritical p. Replace u^p by the value of u^p at a shifted point x+e. Is there still no positive solution, for every subcritical p?
math: Let $n\ge3$, $1<p<\frac{n+2}{n-2}$, $e\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$. Prove or disprove: there is no positive $u\in C^2(\mathbb R^n)$ with $-\Delta u(x)=u(x+e)^p$ for all $x$. (For $1<p<\frac n{n-2}$ the standard Mitidieri–Pohozaev test-function argument applies, since the shift is negligible at large scales; the open range is $\frac n{n-2}\le p<\frac{n+2}{n-2}$. One may also ask whether positive solutions exist for $p\ge\frac{n+2}{n-2}$.)

title: Mass-critical scattering on flat cones
credit: B. Dodson, global well-posedness and scattering for the defocusing L^2-critical NLS in d=2 (Duke Math. J. 2016)
results: Both trivial cases check out. For alpha=2pi/k, C_alpha=R^2/Z_k: the Friedrichs modes e^{ikmθ} with Bessel order k|m| match the Z_k-invariant plane functions, and Dodson applies for any mass, with mass scaled by k. For radial data the m=0 mode on the cone is the 2D radial Laplacian. The sign convention iu_t+Δu=+|u|^2u is defocusing.
plain: Dodson proved that the defocusing cubic Schrodinger equation in the plane scatters for every finite-mass initial state. Prove the same on every flat cone, a plane with a single conical singularity of total angle alpha. For alpha = 2pi/k it follows from Dodson by symmetry, and radial data are also easy. Every other angle, such as the surface of a cube corner (alpha = 3pi/2) or alpha > 2pi, is open.
math: For $\alpha>0$ let $\mathcal C_\alpha=(0,\infty)\times(\mathbb R/\alpha\mathbb Z)$ with metric $dr^2+r^2d\theta^2$ and $\Delta$ the Friedrichs extension of the Laplacian on $C_c^\infty(\mathcal C_\alpha)$. Prove that for every $\alpha>0$ and every $u_0\in L^2(\mathcal C_\alpha)$ the solution of $iu_t+\Delta u=|u|^2u$, $u(0)=u_0$, is global with $\|u\|_{L^4_{t,x}(\mathbb R\times\mathcal C_\alpha)}<\infty$, hence scatters in $L^2$. (Known: $\alpha=2\pi/k$, since $\mathcal C_{2\pi/k}=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z_k$ and Dodson applies to $\mathbb Z_k$-invariant data. Radial data for any $\alpha$, since the radial equation coincides with the 2D one.)

open Classical

abbrev Box (n : ℕ) : Type :=
  {p : Fin (n + 1) × Fin (n + 1) × Fin (n + 1) //

def coords {n : ℕ} (a : Box n) : ℕ × ℕ × ℕ := ((a.1.1 : ℕ), (a.1.2.1 : ℕ), (a.1.2.2 : ℕ))

def Adj (p r : ℕ × ℕ × ℕ) : Prop :=
  |(p.1 : ℤ) - (r.1 : ℤ)| + |(p.2.1 : ℤ) - (r.2.1 : ℤ)| + |(p.2.2 : ℤ) - (r.2.2 : ℤ)| = 1

def spin (b : Bool) : ℝ := if b then 1 else -1

/-- Critical inverse temperature of the square-lattice Ising model. -/
noncomputable def betaC : ℝ := Real.log (1 + Real.sqrt 2) / 2

/-- Sum over ordered adjacent pairs of `σ_a σ_c` (each edge counted twice). -/
noncomputable def energy {n : ℕ} (σ : Box n → Bool) : ℝ :=
  ∑ a : Box n, ∑ c : Box n, if Adj (coords a) (coords c) then spin (σ a) * spin (σ c) else 0

/-- Boltzmann weight at β_c (the factor 1/2 compensates the double counting). -/
noncomputable def weight {n : ℕ} (σ : Box n → Bool) : ℝ := Real.exp (betaC / 2 * energy σ)

/-- Spin at a point of ℕ³ (zero if the point is not a vertex of the box). -/
noncomputable def spinAt {n : ℕ} (σ : Box n → Bool) (x : ℕ × ℕ × ℕ) : ℝ :=
  ∑ a : Box n, if coords a = x then spin (σ a) else 0

/-- Finite-volume free-boundary correlation ⟨σ_o σ_x⟩ on `Box n`. -/
noncomputable def corr (n : ℕ) (x : ℕ × ℕ × ℕ) : ℝ :=
  (∑ σ : Box n → Bool, spinAt σ (0, 0, 0) * spinAt σ x * weight σ) /
    (∑ σ : Box n → Bool, weight σ)

/-- ℓ¹ norm. -/
def norm1 (x : ℕ × ℕ × ℕ) : ℝ := ((x.1 + x.2.1 + x.2.2 : ℕ) : ℝ)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ c C : ℝ, 0 < c ∧ 0 < C ∧ ∃ R : ℕ, 1 ≤ R ∧
    ∀ x : ℕ × ℕ × ℕ, OnSurface x → R ≤ x.1 + x.2.1 + x.2.2 →
      ∀ᶠ n in Filter.atTop,
        c * norm1 x ^ (-(7 : ℝ) / 24) ≤ corr n x ∧ corr n x ≤ C * norm1 x ^ (-(7 : ℝ) / 24)

end OpenProblems.QEDM099
prov_reason: This extends the Chelkak-Hongler-Izyurov conformal-invariance theorem for planar Ising spin correlations to a cone singularity (angle 3pi/2), and no source poses the apex exponent.

title: Alternating quotients of knot groups
credit: Dunfield-Thurston, Finite covers of random 3-manifolds, Invent. Math. 2006 (arXiv:math/0502567), question on alternating quotients; Everitt / Liebeck-Shalev for Fuchsian groups
results: Computer-verified in a fresh script: trefoil (xyx=yxy) surjects onto A5 but not A6 or A7. Figure-eight (w=x^-1yxy^-1) surjects onto A4 and A6 but not A5, A7 or A8, and has no S3 quotient, as det=5 requires. n>=9 not rerun (would take more than 30s). The trefoil argument (centre maps trivially, factor through C2*C3, Miller's (2,3)-generation) is correct.
plain: The trefoil's group maps onto every alternating group A_n with n>=9, because modulo its centre it is the modular group. Show that every nontrivial knot group maps onto A_n for all large n, or at least for infinitely many n, and bound the last exception in terms of the knot.
math: Let $K\subset S^3$ be a nontrivial knot and $G_K=\pi_1(S^3\setminus K)$. (a) Prove that $G_K$ surjects onto $A_n$ for all $n\ge N(K)$, and bound $N(K)$ in terms of the crossing number. (b) Weaker: prove that $G_K$ surjects onto $A_n$ for infinitely many $n$, or even for one $n\ge5$. Data (exhaustive search over pairs of conjugate even permutations, meridians $x,y$ with $wx=yw$): for the trefoil ($w=xy$) a surjection exists exactly for $n=5$ and $n\ge9$, since every surjection kills the centre and factors through $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb Z)\cong C_2*C_3$, and Miller proved $(2,3)$-generation of $A_n$ for $n\ne3,6,7,8$. For the figure-eight knot ($w=x^{-1}yxy^{-1}$) a surjection exists for $n=6,9,10$ and not for $n=5,7,8$. Is $N(4_1)=9$, i.e. does $G_{4_1}$ surject onto $A_n$ for every $n\ge9$?
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-M100: Alternating quotients of knot groups
The trefoil group surjects onto every alternating group A_n with n >= 9 (and onto A_5),
because it maps onto the modular group. Does every nontrivial knot group surject onto A_n for
all sufficiently large n?
Informal statement: Let K ⊂ S^3 be a nontrivial knot and G_K = π_1(S^3 \ K). (a) Prove that
G_K surjects onto A_n for all n >= N(K) (and bound N(K) in terms of the crossing number).
(b, weaker) Prove that G_K surjects onto A_n for infinitely many n.
Formalization notes: Only the main question (a), existence of N(K), is formalized; the request
to bound N(K) by the crossing number, the weaker variants (b), and the specific question
N(4_1) = 9 are not. Knots are tame: a knot is a subset K of R^3 = `Fin 3 → ℝ` that is a finite
union of straight segments and is homeomorphic to the unit circle (a polygonal knot). Every
tame knot is ambient isotopic to a polygonal one, and the knot group is the same whether the
complement is taken in R^3 or in S^3 (removing a point from a 3-manifold does not change π_1).
"Nontrivial" is encoded as: the knot group is not isomorphic to ℤ. By Dehn's lemma
(Papakyriakopoulos) this is equivalent to K not being the unknot. The basepoint x₀ is arbitrary
(the complement is path-connected, so the group does not depend on it up to isomorphism).
Proving Claim answers (a) affirmatively; proving ¬Claim means exhibiting a nontrivial polygonal
knot whose group fails to surject onto A_n for infinitely many n.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM100

/-- Three-dimensional real space as a function type (product topology = Euclidean). -/
abbrev R3 : Type := Fin 3 → ℝ

/-- The unit circle in the plane. -/
def unitCircle : Set (Fin 2 → ℝ) := {p | p 0 ^ 2 + p 1 ^ 2 = 1}

/-- A polygonal (hence tame) knot: a finite union of segments homeomorphic to a circle. -/
def IsPolygonalKnot (K : Set R3) : Prop :=
  (∃ S : Finset (R3 × R3), K = ⋃ s ∈ S, segment ℝ s.1 s.2) ∧
  Nonempty (↥K ≃ₜ ↥unitCircle)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ K : Set R3, IsPolygonalKnot K → ∀ x₀ : ↥(Kᶜ),
    IsEmpty (FundamentalGroup ↥(Kᶜ) x₀ ≃* Multiplicative ℤ) →
      ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ n : ℕ, N ≤ n →
        ∃ f : FundamentalGroup ↥(Kᶜ) x₀ →* ↥(alternatingGroup (Fin n)),
          Function.Surjective f

end OpenProblems.QEDM100
prov_reason: Dunfield-Thurston asked whether hyperbolic 3-manifold groups have alternating quotients; this specializes to knot groups (including non-hyperbolic knots) and strengthens it to all sufficiently large n with an effective threshold.

title: Infinitely many knot types in the symmetric ABC flow
credit: Etnyre & Ghrist (2000), arXiv:math-ph/9906021; Enciso, Peralta-Salas (and Romaniega), arXiv:2006.15033.
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.17449 (Szumiński–Llibre, 2026 preprint): cited only as related perturbative work; nothing in the statement depends on it.
plain: Steady Euler flows can carry knotted streamlines, and generic high-frequency Beltrami fields on the torus contain every knot. Show that the most-studied explicit example, the ABC flow with A = B = C = 1, has closed streamlines tied in infinitely many different knots.
math: Let $X=(\sin z+\cos y,\ \sin x+\cos z,\ \sin y+\cos x)$ on $\mathbb T^3=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^3$ (a curl eigenfield, $\nabla\times X=X$). Prove that the periodic orbits of $X$ that lie in some embedded 3-ball $B\subset\mathbb T^3$ realize infinitely many distinct knot types (as knots in $B\cong$ a ball in $\mathbb R^3$). Stronger: every knot type is realized.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-M101: Infinitely many knot types in the symmetric ABC flow
Steady Euler flows can carry knotted streamlines. Show that the ABC flow with A = B = C = 1 on the 3-torus has closed
streamlines, each lying in an embedded ball, tied in infinitely many different knot types.
Informal statement: Let X = (sin z + cos y, sin x + cos z, sin y + cos x) on 𝕋³ = (ℝ/2πℤ)³. Prove that the periodic
orbits of X that lie in some embedded 3-ball B ⊂ 𝕋³ realize infinitely many distinct knot types (as knots in
B ≅ a ball in ℝ³). (Stronger, not formalized here: every knot type is realized.)
Formalization notes: Work on the universal cover ℝ³ = (Fin 3 → ℝ) with the 2π-periodic field `abc`. A closed orbit of
X in 𝕋³ lying in an embedded ball lifts to a genuinely periodic, non-constant integral curve γ of `abc` in ℝ³
contained in a lifted ball B̃ on which the projection to 𝕋³ is injective (`InjectiveModLattice`); conversely such a
γ projects to a closed orbit in an embedded ball. Balls are taken tame: B̃ = h(closed unit ball) for a homeomorphism h
of ℝ³ (every smooth or PL ball is of this form). The knot type of the orbit in B is then the ambient-isotopy class
in ℝ³ of the lifted curve. `KnotEquiv` is ambient isotopy: a jointly continuous family of homeomorphisms H_t of ℝ³
with H_0 = id carrying K₁ onto K₂ (orientation-preserving, so a chiral knot and its mirror are different types; this
is the standard notion, and for these smooth knots it agrees with equivalence under orientation-preserving
homeomorphisms). Claim: there is a sequence of such orbit-knots, pairwise not ambient isotopic. Proving Claim = the
result; proving ¬Claim = only finitely many knot types occur among ball-contained closed orbits.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM101

/-- The ABC field with `A = B = C = 1`, as a `2π`-periodic field on `ℝ³`. -/
noncomputable def abc (x : Fin 3 → ℝ) : Fin 3 → ℝ :=
  ![Real.sin (x 2) + Real.cos (x 1), Real.sin (x 0) + Real.cos (x 2), Real.sin (x 1) + Real.cos (x 0)]

/-- The projection `ℝ³ → 𝕋³ = (ℝ/2πℤ)³` is injective on `B`. -/
def InjectiveModLattice (B : Set (Fin 3 → ℝ)) : Prop :=
  ∀ a ∈ B, ∀ b ∈ B, (∀ i : Fin 3, ∃ k : ℤ, a i - b i = 2 * Real.pi * (k : ℝ)) → a = b

/-- `B` is a tame closed 3-ball in `ℝ³` that projects injectively to the torus. -/
def IsTameBallInTorus (B : Set (Fin 3 → ℝ)) : Prop :=
  (∃ h : (Fin 3 → ℝ) ≃ₜ (Fin 3 → ℝ), B = h '' Metric.closedBall (0 : Fin 3 → ℝ) 1) ∧
    InjectiveModLattice B

/-- `K` is the image of a non-constant periodic integral curve of `abc` in `ℝ³`. -/
def IsClosedOrbit (K : Set (Fin 3 → ℝ)) : Prop :=
  ∃ γ : ℝ → (Fin 3 → ℝ), ∃ T : ℝ, 0 < T ∧
    (∀ t : ℝ, HasDerivAt γ (abc (γ t)) t) ∧ (∀ t : ℝ, γ (t + T) = γ t) ∧
    (∃ t₁ t₂ : ℝ, γ t₁ ≠ γ t₂) ∧ K = Set.range γ

/-- A closed orbit lying in a tame ball of the torus (lifted to `ℝ³`). -/
def IsBallOrbitKnot (K : Set (Fin 3 → ℝ)) : Prop :=
  IsClosedOrbit K ∧ ∃ B : Set (Fin 3 → ℝ), IsTameBallInTorus B ∧ K ⊆ B

/-- Ambient isotopy of subsets of `ℝ³`. -/
def KnotEquiv (K₁ K₂ : Set (Fin 3 → ℝ)) : Prop :=
  ∃ H : ℝ → (Fin 3 → ℝ) ≃ₜ (Fin 3 → ℝ),
    Continuous (fun p : ℝ × (Fin 3 → ℝ) => H p.1 p.2) ∧
    (∀ x : Fin 3 → ℝ, H 0 x = x) ∧ (H 1) '' K₁ = K₂

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ K : ℕ → Set (Fin 3 → ℝ), (∀ n : ℕ, IsBallOrbitKnot (K n)) ∧
    ∀ m n : ℕ, m ≠ n → ¬ KnotEquiv (K m) (K n)

end OpenProblems.QEDM101
prov_reason: All-knots theorems exist for perturbed or random high-frequency Beltrami/Euler flows; asking it for the explicit symmetric ABC field is a new, specific case not posed in the refs.

title: Knotted billiards in a regular tetrahedron
credit: Extends Jones–Przytycki (Lissajous knots and billiard knots, 1998) and Koseleff–Pecker, 'Every knot is a billiard knot', arXiv:1106.5600; periodic orbits in polyhedra: Bedaride–Rao arXiv:1104.1051.
plain: A billiard ball bouncing periodically inside a regular tetrahedron, without hitting edges or corners, traces a closed polygon in space. Is any such polygon knotted, and do infinitely many different knot types occur?
math: Call a periodic billiard trajectory in a regular tetrahedron $T\subset\mathbb R^3$ admissible if it never meets an edge or vertex of $T$ and its image is an embedded closed polygon. (a) Does some admissible trajectory form a nontrivial knot? (b) Prove that the set of knot types of admissible periodic trajectories is infinite.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-M102: Knotted billiards in a regular tetrahedron
A billiard ball bouncing periodically inside a regular tetrahedron, never hitting an edge or a
corner, traces a closed polygon in space. Do infinitely many knot types occur among these
polygons (in particular, is any of them knotted)?
Informal statement: Call a periodic billiard trajectory in a regular tetrahedron T ⊂ ℝ³
admissible if it never meets an edge or vertex of T and its image is an embedded closed polygon.
(a) Does some admissible trajectory form a nontrivial knot? (b) Prove that the set of knot types
of admissible periodic trajectories is infinite. The Claim is (b), which implies (a).
Formalization notes: T = {x ∈ ℝ³ : ⟪x, vᵢ⟫ ≥ −1 for i = 0..3} with vertices
v₀ = (1,1,1), v₁ = (1,−1,−1), v₂ = (−1,1,−1), v₃ = (−1,−1,1); face i is {⟪x, vᵢ⟫ = −1}, with
outward normal −vᵢ. A periodic trajectory (`PeriodicOrbit`) is an N-periodic sequence of bounce
points pₖ (N ≥ 1), each in the relative interior of a face φ(k) (on that face and strictly inside
the other three half-spaces, so never on an edge or vertex), consecutive bounce points on
different faces (so the open chords lie in the interior of T, by convexity), and the reflection
law: the outgoing direction p_{k+2} − p_{k+1} is a positive multiple of the mirror image of the
incoming direction p_{k+1} − p_k in the plane of face φ(k+1), R(d) = d − (2/3)⟪d, v⟫ v. The
image is ⋃_{k<N} [pₖ, p_{k+1}]; admissible means it is a topological circle (image of a
continuous injective map from the unit circle in ℂ). This automatically discards orbits that
retrace themselves or self-intersect; orbits traversing their image twice are allowed, as in the
notes. Knot types are compared up to homeomorphisms of ℝ³ (`KnotEquiv`): for polygonal (tame)
knots this is ambient isotopy up to mirror image, and since each such class contains at most two
isotopy classes, "infinitely many knot types" and "nontrivial knot" mean the same under either
convention. The unknot is represented by a planar triangle. Proving `Claim` = exhibiting, for
every n, n admissible orbits with pairwise inequivalent images; `¬Claim` = only finitely many
knot types occur.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM102
noncomputable section

/-- Points of ℝ³. -/
abbrev R3 : Type := Fin 3 → ℝ

/-- Euclidean inner product on ℝ³. -/
def dot (x y : R3) : ℝ := ∑ i : Fin 3, x i * y i

/-- Vertices of the regular tetrahedron `T`. -/
def tetVert : Fin 4 → R3 :=
  ![![(1 : ℝ), 1, 1], ![(1 : ℝ), -1, -1], ![(-1 : ℝ), 1, -1], ![(-1 : ℝ), -1, 1]]

/-- The regular tetrahedron `T = {x | ∀ i, ⟪x, vᵢ⟫ ≥ −1}`. -/
def tetra : Set R3 := {x : R3 | ∀ i : Fin 4, -1 ≤ dot x (tetVert i)}

/-- `p` lies in the relative interior of face `i` (the face opposite vertex `i`). -/
def OnFaceInt (i : Fin 4) (p : R3) : Prop :=
  dot p (tetVert i) = -1 ∧ ∀ j : Fin 4, j ≠ i → -1 < dot p (tetVert j)

/-- Reflection of a direction vector in the plane of face `i` (normal `vᵢ`, `‖vᵢ‖² = 3`). -/
def refl (i : Fin 4) (d : R3) : R3 :=
  d - ((2 : ℝ) / 3 * dot d (tetVert i)) • tetVert i

/-- A periodic billiard trajectory in `T` avoiding edges and vertices. -/
structure PeriodicOrbit where
  N : ℕ
  hN : 0 < N
  p : ℕ → R3
  face : ℕ → Fin 4
  periodic : ∀ k, p (k + N) = p k
  on_face : ∀ k, OnFaceInt (face k) (p k)
  next_face : ∀ k, face (k + 1) ≠ face k
  reflection : ∀ k, ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧
    p (k + 2) - p (k + 1) = c • refl (face (k + 1)) (p (k + 1) - p k)

/-- The image of the trajectory: the union of its chords over one period. -/
def PeriodicOrbit.image (o : PeriodicOrbit) : Set R3 :=
  ⋃ k : Fin o.N, segment ℝ (o.p (k : ℕ)) (o.p ((k : ℕ) + 1))

/-- The image is an embedded closed curve (homeomorphic to a circle). -/
def PeriodicOrbit.Admissible (o : PeriodicOrbit) : Prop :=
  ∃ γ : Metric.sphere (0 : ℂ) 1 → R3,
    Continuous γ ∧ Function.Injective γ ∧ Set.range γ = o.image

/-- Knot equivalence up to homeomorphism of ℝ³. -/
def KnotEquiv (K₁ K₂ : Set R3) : Prop :=
  ∃ h : R3 ≃ₜ R3, h '' K₁ = K₂

/-- A planar triangle, representing the unknot. -/
def unknot : Set R3 :=
  segment ℝ (0 : R3) (Pi.single 0 1) ∪ segment ℝ (Pi.single 0 1) (Pi.single 1 1) ∪
    segment ℝ (Pi.single 1 1) (0 : R3)

/-- Part (a), implied by `Claim`: some admissible orbit is knotted. (Not the Claim.) -/
def SomeKnottedOrbit : Prop :=
  ∃ o : PeriodicOrbit, o.Admissible ∧ ¬ KnotEquiv o.image unknot

/-- Part (b): infinitely many knot types occur among admissible periodic orbits. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ n : ℕ, ∃ o : Fin n → PeriodicOrbit, (∀ i, (o i).Admissible) ∧
    ∀ i j : Fin n, i ≠ j → ¬ KnotEquiv (o i).image (o j).image

end

end OpenProblems.QEDM102
M_fix_reason: M is well posed; Lean takes (b) as the Claim since (b) implies (a). Note for reviewers: if (a) alone is wanted as a separate problem, `SomeKnottedOrbit` is provided.
prov_reason: Transfers the cube billiard-knot (Lissajous knot) question to the regular tetrahedron; searches found work on billiard knots in cubes/cylinders and periodic orbits in polyhedra/simplices but no knot-type results for the tetrahedron.
